newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka economy seen reviving in 1997 - ADB.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka economy seen reviving in 1997 - ADB.

text.p: Sri Lanka's economy will bounce back this year, given favourable weather, after slowing down in 1996 because of war, drought and power cuts, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said on Thursday.

The economy is projected to grow nearly six percent in 1997 and 1998 after gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1996 slowed to 3.8 percent, much lower than the previous year's 5.6 percent, the ADB said in its annual report.
The central bank has put 1995 growth at a provisional 5.5 percent.
"The year 1996 was difficult for Sri Lanka," the ADB said. "Drought and civil war reduced economic growth and exports, and the inflation rate virtually doubled."
The slowdown was mainly due to problems in the agricultural sector, which shrank by 0.9 percent, and power shortages, which hit manufacturing, the report said.

Sri Lanka endured daily power cuts of up to eight hours at the height of last year's drought after water levels in hydroreservoirs, which supply most of the electricity, plunged to dangerously low levels with the failure of monsoon rains.

The country also faces the prospect of a power crisis this year after hydroreservoir water levels fell with the failure of the November-March northeast monsoon for the second straight year, and weak intermonsoon showers.
The ADB said paddy output fell by 23 percent in 1996, forcing the Indian Ocean island to import 350,000 tonnes of rice.

The industry sector, accounting for about one third of GDP, grew by only 6.2 percent because of the slow growth of the manufacturing subsector, which suffered from prolonged power cuts in the second quarter of the year, it said.
The report did not give comparative figures for industry sector growth.
Though 1996 exports rose by 12 percent to $4.2 billion despite the poor performance of the manufacturing sector, the growth rate was lower than the 18.4 percent recorded in 1995, it said.
The ADB forecast exports will grow by 17 percent to $4.97 billion this year and rise above five billion dollars in 1998.

The 1996 budget deficit rose to nine percent of GDP from 8.4 percent in 1995, lifted mainly by a sharp rise in defence spending to finance the government's war, now in its 14th year, with Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, it said.
The LTTE are fighting for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in the island's north and east.

Sri Lanka had planned to cut its budget deficit to 7.8 percent of GDP in 1996 but a 40 percent rise in defence spending, the doubling of the wheat subsidy and a slowdown in revenues due to an easing of industrial activity forced the deficit up to nine percent, it said.
The rate of monetary expansion remained high in 1996, with broad money supply (M2) expanding by 18 percent, mainly because of heavy government borrowing to fund the war, it said.
The ADB projected inflation to slow to 10 percent this year and eight percent in 1998, after rising sharply to 15.9 percent in 1996 from 7.7 percent the previous year.
"Pressure on prices is likely to be strong in the first half of 1997 owing to the upward revision of state-administered prices and depreciation of the Sri Lanka rupee," it said.
"Increases in salaries of civil servants over two years will also exert upward pressure on prices," the ADB report added.
It said peace and political stability will largely determine the level of foreign direct investment in the next two years.

"Provided that the civil war does not flare up again, and that no major labour union problems -- recurrent features of the economic landscape -- re-emerge, a resurgence of investment can be expected," it said.
